title: How to Get Started: Your 30-Minute Launch Blueprint
summary: A practical step-by-step launch plan covering account checks, SharePoint folder setup, picking your first high-value use case, and running a 3-question smoke test.

intro.what: Do not start by trying to automate your hardest workflow on day one. Follow a structured 30-minute launch sequence that guarantees early wins and zero data leaks.
intro.features: Combines a 2-minute license & browser check, a 10-minute SharePoint folder cleanup, a 10-minute Level 2 prototype, and a 3-minute smoke test.
intro.m365: Create one clean SharePoint folder ('Copilot-Approved-SOPs') containing only current, approved policies—never point an agent at a messy shared drive full of 2019 drafts.
intro.exchange: Pick one repetitive question your team answers 10+ times a week by email or phone as your very first agent.
intro.developer: Follow the 5-Level Agent Ladder: start in Agent Builder (Levels 1–3) and only move to Copilot Studio (Levels 4–5) once your Q&A rules are rock-solid.
sources: Microsoft Learn · Best practices for building declarative agents

sections.title: Five Practical Steps Before You Build Your First Real Agent
paragraphs: Step 1 — Run the 2-Minute License & Browser Check: Confirm you can sign in to m365.cloud.microsoft/chat and see 'Create an agent' in the left sidebar. Bookmark that page so you never waste time hunting for the button.

Step 2 — Pick One High-Friction, Low-Risk Use Case: Choose a task where rules are already written down, questions happen repeatedly, and wrong guesses waste staff time—such as visitor permit rates, shuttle hours, citation appeal deadlines, or shift handoff formatting.

Step 3 — Prepare a Clean SharePoint Folder ('Copilot-Approved-SOPs'): Create a dedicated folder on your team's SharePoint site. Put only the active, approved handbook or rate sheet inside it, and give every rule a short ID like [Rule VP-01]. Move outdated drafts into a separate 'Archive' folder outside the agent's reach.

Step 4 — Build a Level 1 or Level 2 Prototype First: Open Agent Builder, paste clear numbered Instructions, attach your clean SharePoint folder, and toggle Web Search OFF so the agent cannot pull outside rules.

Step 5 — Run the 3-Question Smoke Test Before Sharing: Test (a) one standard question from page 1, (b) one tricky edge case, and (c) one topic NOT in your files to prove the agent says 'Not covered in our current handbook' instead of guessing.

sections.title: How Agent Builder and Copilot Studio Fit Together
paragraphs: Microsoft powers both Agent Builder and the full Copilot Studio workshop using the exact same underlying Copilot Studio engine. When you click 'Create an agent' inside Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, you are using the streamlined, no-code Agent Builder interface.

If you later outgrow Agent Builder—for example, when you want your agent to ask 4 intake questions in strict order and append a row into Excel Online—you simply open copilotstudio.microsoft.com (or click 'Open in Copilot Studio') and continue enhancing the exact same agent without starting over.

title: 2026 Licensing Guide: What Licenses Are Required?
summary: A clear, jargon-free breakdown of Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, included Copilot Chat rights, and Copilot Studio credit packs or pay-as-you-go meters.

intro.what: Microsoft licenses Copilot agents through two main mechanisms: per-user seat subscriptions (Microsoft 365 Copilot) and tenant-wide usage meters (Copilot Studio Copilot Credits).
intro.features: If you hold a paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seat ($30/user/month, or $21/user/month for Copilot Business up to 300 users), building and using internal agents inside Teams, SharePoint, and M365 Copilot is included at no extra per-message fee.
intro.m365: Every user still requires a qualifying Microsoft 365 base subscription (such as Business Basic/Standard/Premium, E3, E5, F1, or F3) for Entra ID identity, SharePoint, and Teams access.
intro.exchange: Staff without a $30 M365 Copilot seat can still use Copilot Chat at no extra charge, and can run shared agents if IT links a Copilot Studio Credit Pack or Azure Pay-As-You-Go meter.
intro.developer: Authoring in Copilot Studio uses a $0 Copilot Studio User Author license (or Copilot Author role) paired with either a 25,000 Copilot Credits/month tenant pack, an Azure Pay-As-You-Go billing plan, or a Pre-Purchase Plan (P3).
sources: Microsoft Learn · Microsoft Copilot Studio Licensing & Billing
Microsoft Learn · Manage Copilot Credits and capacity

sections.title: The Three Real-World Licensing Scenarios Explained
paragraphs: Licensing is often the most confusing part of rolling out Copilot agents because Microsoft supports both named-user seats and shared consumption pools. Here is how the three real-world setups work in 2026:

Scenario 1 — You Hold a Full Microsoft 365 Copilot Seat ($30/user/month, or $21/user/month on Copilot Business): You have full access for internal team agents. You can open Agent Builder, attach SharePoint folders, build custom declarative agents, and use agents published to Teams, SharePoint, and Microsoft 365 Copilot with no separate per-message meter for internal M365 grounding.

Scenario 2 — You Only Have a Base Microsoft 365 Plan (E3, E5, Business Standard, F3, etc.) Without the $30 Add-On: You still get Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat included at no extra cost for web-grounded chat. However, to build or run custom agents that ground in SharePoint files or execute actions, your IT administrator must link a Copilot Studio consumption meter (Pay-As-You-Go via Azure, or a prepaid Copilot Credit capacity pack) to your environment.

Scenario 3 — You Build Autonomous Background Triggers or Public-Facing Agents (Copilot Studio): Whenever an agent wakes up on its own without a human user typing in chat (for example, monitoring a SharePoint list 24/7 and posting Teams alerts) or serves external website visitors, it consumes Copilot Credits from a tenant capacity pack (25,000 credits/month per pack) or Pay-As-You-Go meter—even if the builder holds a $30 M365 Copilot license.

title: How an End User Can Verify Their License & Access (2-Minute Self-Check)
summary: Follow four quick browser checks any everyday end user can run—with zero IT admin privileges—to confirm your exact license and agent permissions.
where: Open your work browser (Edge, Chrome, or Safari) signed in to your organization's Microsoft 365 account.

actions.title: Check 1: Inspect Your Assigned Subscriptions (myaccount.microsoft.com)
actions.do: Go to https://myaccount.microsoft.com and click Subscriptions (or View subscriptions) in the left menu. Scan the list for 'Microsoft 365 Copilot', 'Microsoft 365 Copilot Business', 'Microsoft 365 E7', or 'Microsoft Copilot Studio'.
actions.see: You see your exact assigned product names. If 'Microsoft 365 Copilot' is listed, you have full per-seat Agent Builder and internal agent rights.
actions.stuck: If only 'Microsoft 365 E3/E5' or 'Business Standard' appears, you do not have a dedicated $30 Copilot seat yet—proceed to Check 2 to see if IT enabled tenant-wide Agent Builder or Pay-As-You-Go access.

actions.title: Check 2: Test the 'Create an Agent' Door in Copilot Chat
actions.do: Open https://m365.cloud.microsoft/chat and expand the left-hand navigation panel. Look for 'Agents' and 'Create an agent' (or 'New agent'). Click it and open the Configure tab.
actions.see: If the split-screen Agent Builder opens and the Knowledge section lets you browse SharePoint/OneDrive files, your account is ready for Levels 1–3 immediately.
actions.stuck: If 'Create an agent' is missing or greyed out, your IT admin has restricted agent authoring in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center Integrated Apps settings.

actions.title: Check 3: Check Your Copilot Studio Author Access & Environment
actions.do: Open https://copilotstudio.microsoft.com in a new tab. Look at the top-right Environment picker and click the Settings gear icon -> Plan / Licensing (or try clicking + Create -> New agent).
actions.see: If you land on the Copilot Studio Home workspace and can open 'New agent', you have active Copilot Studio authoring rights (either via your M365 Copilot seat or a $0 Copilot Studio User License + environment billing plan).
actions.stuck: If a prompt asks you to 'Start a free trial' or says 'Contact your admin for a license,' you lack either the $0 Copilot Studio User License or an active tenant credit/PAYG plan.

actions.title: Check 4: Verify SharePoint Knowledge Access (The Two-Lock Check)
actions.do: Open your team's SharePoint library in the browser and verify you can open and read the handbook files you plan to use.
actions.see: You can view the files cleanly without requesting access. Remember: an agent can only read SharePoint files you yourself can open.
actions.stuck: If you get 'Access Denied' in SharePoint, ask your team lead or site owner for Read/View access before building your agent.

sections.title: Copy-Paste Email to Send IT If Anything Is Missing
paragraphs: If Checks 1–3 show that 'Create an agent' or Copilot Studio is blocked on your account, you do not need to guess technical license names. Copy and send this short note to your IT Help Desk so they can turn on the exact right toggle in two minutes:

"Hi IT Team — I am building a team knowledge helper in Microsoft 365 Copilot. Could you please verify: (1) That my account has either a Microsoft 365 Copilot license OR a $0 Copilot Studio User License / Copilot Author role assigned, (2) That 'Create an agent' (Agent Builder) is enabled for my user group in the M365 Admin Center, and (3) Which shared SharePoint library we should use for approved team SOPs? Thank you!"

title: Author Deterministic System Instructions & Guardrails
summary: Write structured, anti-hallucination system instructions with explicit fallback clauses and output schemas.

actions.title: Define Role, Scope, and Output Contract

actions.see: Clear section delimiters prevent instruction drift across multi-turn chats.
actions.stuck: Keep system instructions concise and unambiguous; avoid conflicting directives.

actions.title: Disable ungrounded fallback behavior
actions.do: Add explicit negative constraints: 'Do NOT extrapolate, infer unstated SLAs, or use parametric world knowledge. Return UNSPECIFIED for null fields.'

actions.stuck: Test with adversarial prompts asking for unstated fees or exceptions.

actions.see: Reduces prompt-engineering variance among end users.
actions.stuck: Keep starter titles concise (<40 chars).

actions.do: Submit an incomplete incident payload and verify null fields output UNSPECIFIED rather than fabricated timestamps.
actions.see: Deterministic refusal confirms prompt resilience.
actions.stuck: Re-test after any model or instruction revision.
